lead: Trap a particle between two rigid walls and its energy can no longer take any value. Only certain standing waves fit between the walls, so the allowed energies form a ladder: E₁, 4E₁, 9E₁ and so on. This is the particle in a box, the simplest problem where quantisation comes straight out of a boundary condition. The same idea in three dimensions explains the colours of quantum dots, the absorption of conjugated dye molecules and the level spacing in semiconductor nanostructures.
prereq: You need: the time-independent Schrodinger equation from 6.7, the Born meaning of |ψ|² from 6.6, the uncertainty principle from 6.5, boundary conditions and simple trigonometry.

sections.h3: The infinite well: a particle that cannot escape

blocks.text: Put a particle of mass m on the x-axis and trap it between rigid walls at x = 0 and x = L. Inside the box the potential energy is zero: V(x) = 0 for 0 < x < L. Outside, V = ∞, so the particle is never found there. This model is the infinite square well, or particle in a box.

Infinite potential outside means ψ = 0 outside. The wavefunction must be continuous at the walls, so ψ(0) = 0 and ψ(L) = 0. These two boundary conditions do the real work: they replace a continuous range of energies with a discrete list.

blocks.where: ℏ = h/2π is the reduced Planck constant, 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; m is the particle mass in kg; E is the total energy in joules; ψ(x) is the wavefunction.

blocks.text: Write k² = 2mE/ℏ². Then d²ψ/dx² = −k²ψ, whose general solution is ψ = A sin kx + B cos kx, with A and B constants.

Apply ψ(0) = 0: B = 0, leaving ψ = A sin kx. Apply ψ(L) = 0: A sin kL = 0. A = 0 gives no particle at all, so sin kL = 0 and kL = nπ with n = 1, 2, 3, … The value n = 0 gives ψ = 0 everywhere and is rejected. Only wavelengths with k = nπ/L fit between the walls.

blocks.where: ψn is the normalised wavefunction of level n; L is the full box width in metres; x is position in metres. The factor √(2/L) comes from setting ∫|ψn|²dx = 1 between 0 and L.
En is the energy of level n in joules; h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant; m is the particle mass in kg; L is the box width in metres; n = 1, 2, 3, … is the quantum number.

blocks.text: The lowest energy E1 = h²/(8mL²) is not zero. Confining the particle to a width L makes Δx of order L, so the uncertainty principle forces Δp ≥ ℏ/2L and the kinetic energy cannot vanish. This minimum is the zero-point energy.

Nodes: ψn has n − 1 zeros strictly inside the box. ψ1 is a single hump, ψ2 crosses zero at x = L/2, ψ3 crosses at L/3 and 2L/3. The probability density |ψn|² = (2/L) sin²(nπx/L) has n humps, so a highly excited particle is almost equally likely anywhere in the box.
Level spacing grows: En+1 − En = (2n + 1)h²/(8mL²). Gaps widen with n, unlike the equal gaps of a harmonic oscillator. The figure plots the first three wavefunctions.
For a rectangular box with sides Lx, Ly, Lz, take V = 0 inside and ∞ outside, and write ψ(x, y, z) = X(x)Y(y)Z(z). Each factor obeys a one-dimensional box equation with its own quantum number.

blocks.where: nx, ny, nz = 1, 2, 3, … are the quantum numbers for the three directions; Lx, Ly, Lz are the side lengths in metres; m is the mass in kg; h is Planck's constant.

blocks.text: The wavefunction is a product of three sines, ψ = √(8/V) sin(nxπx/Lx) sin(nyπy/Ly) sin(nzπz/Lz), with V = LxLyLz the box volume. The probability density factorises into three one-dimensional densities.

For a cube, Lx = Ly = Lz = L, so E = (h²/8mL²)(nx² + ny² + nz²). Different quantum-number sets can share the same sum of squares, hence the same energy. The sets (2,1,1), (1,2,1) and (1,1,2) all give 2² + 1² + 1² = 6, so that level is three-fold degenerate. The ground state (1,1,1) is non-degenerate.

Degeneracy follows from symmetry. Stretch the box so Lx ≠ Ly ≠ Lz and the three states separate in energy. The number of states per unit energy range, the density of states, grows in three dimensions and enters the free-electron theory of Unit 7.

sections.h3: Where the box model is used

blocks.text: Real walls are finite. A finite well of depth V0 lets ψ decay exponentially into the walls instead of vanishing there. The energies then lie slightly below the infinite-box values and only a finite number of bound states fit. That exponential tail is what permits escape by tunnelling in 6.9.

items: Conjugated dye molecules: the π electrons move along a chain of length L; a longer chain means smaller E1 and absorption at longer wavelength, which is why such dyes are coloured.
Quantum dots: semiconductor crystals a few nanometres across; their size sets the gap and therefore the emitted colour.
Quantum-well lasers: thin semiconductor layers confine electrons, and the confined levels set the emission wavelength.

blocks.text: Two exam checks: n starts at 1, never 0; and L is the full width between the walls, not the half-width.

figure.caption: The first three wavefunctions of the infinite square well plotted against x/L. Each curve is zero at both walls, and the number of interior nodes is n − 1.

spec.aria: The first three normalized wavefunctions of an infinite square well, with n minus one nodes inside the box.

examples.question: An electron is confined in a one-dimensional infinite box of width L = 1.0 nm. Find the first three energy levels in electron-volts. Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
steps: Write the formula: En = n²h²/(8mL²), so E1 = h²/(8mL²).

traps: Using n = 0. Counting starts at n = 1; n = 0 makes ψ zero everywhere, so no particle exists.
Taking L as half the box width. L is the full distance between the walls; halving it multiplies every energy by 4.
Treating E as proportional to n. It goes as n², so doubling n quadruples the energy.
Mixing ℏ and h. En = n²h²/(8mL²) uses h; starting from −(ℏ²/2m)ψ″ needs ℏ = h/2π before comparing.
Claiming degeneracy for any box. (2,1,1), (1,2,1) and (1,1,2) share an energy only when Lx = Ly = Lz; in a rectangular box they split.

quiz.q: State the boundary conditions for a particle in a one-dimensional infinite well of width L.
quiz.a: ψ(0) = 0 and ψ(L) = 0, because the wavefunction is continuous and vanishes outside the infinite walls.

quiz.q: Write the energy of the nth level of a particle of mass m in an infinite well of width L.
Why is the lowest allowed energy of a confined particle not zero?
quiz.a: Confinement to width L gives Δx of order L, so Δp ≥ ℏ/2L. A nonzero momentum spread means nonzero kinetic energy; the minimum is E1 = h²/(8mL²).

quiz.q: How many interior nodes does ψ4 have, and where are they?
quiz.a: n − 1 = 3 interior nodes, at x = L/4, L/2 and 3L/4.

quiz.q: An electron is in an infinite well of width 0.5 nm. Find E1 in eV, given that a 1.0 nm well has E1 = 0.376 eV.
quiz.a: E1 ∝ 1/L². Halving L multiplies E1 by 4: E1 = 4 × 0.376 = 1.504 eV.

quiz.q: For a cubic box, give the quantum numbers of the first excited level and its degeneracy.
quiz.a: (2,1,1), (1,2,1) and (1,1,2) all give nx² + ny² + nz² = 6, so the energy is 6h²/(8mL²) and the level is three-fold degenerate.

quiz.q: By what factor does the gap E2 − E1 change if the box width is doubled?
quiz.a: Every energy scales as 1/L², so doubling L divides all energies and their differences by 4. The gap becomes one quarter of its original value, (3/4)h²/(8mL²).

beyond: Not for the exam. The particle in a box is the first exactly solvable model of a nanostructure, and its three-dimensional form underlies the density-of-states engineering used in quantum-dot displays and quantum-well lasers. Researchers add strain, magnetic fields and electron-electron interaction to the same box to model nanowires and two-dimensional electron gases. Search quantum dot absorption spectrum, quantum well laser active region, or density of states three-dimensional box to go further.
